Hux could plausibly use a disguised explosive against the Knights of Ren. He is ruthless, ambitious, and willing to use deception against rivals. If the knights became enemies of the First Order, a trap disguised as an artifact would fit his pragmatic approach. The disguise would be clever only if Hux had reason to believe the knights would take the bait. Their interest in dark-side relics makes a holocron plausible, but a crude fake or a suspiciously convenient discovery might alert them. Their Force abilities could also make an explosive harder to conceal. The plan would be most convincing if Hux used a credible artifact and arranged for the knights to find it through a believable source.

A former president has **absolute immunity from criminal prosecution for acts within his exclusive constitutional authority**, and presumptive immunity for other official acts. He has no presidential immunity for unofficial conduct. That is the Supreme Court’s holding in *Trump v. United States* (2024).

A reasonable originalist analysis would begin with the Constitution’s text, structure, and historical understanding. The Constitution does not expressly grant former presidents criminal immunity. Article II nevertheless assigns certain powers exclusively to the president, supporting a strong argument that Congress cannot criminalize a president’s exercise of those powers. Whether the original understanding also supports presumptive immunity for other official conduct is more contested: the Constitution provides mechanisms for accountability, but it does not spell out the criminal-prosecution rule adopted by the Court.

Under the Court’s rule, prosecutors may overcome the presumption for a nonexclusive official act by showing that prosecution would pose no danger of intruding on the authority and functions of the executive branch. Courts must classify the alleged conduct carefully; a prosecutor cannot quickly transform an unofficial act into an official one, or transform an official act into a private one, simply by labeling it. The Court also restricted the use of immune official acts as evidence to prove charges involving unofficial conduct.

The framework can be pictured as a bridge from accusation to trial: one bridge concerns exclusive powers, one bridge other official acts, one bridge unofficial conduct, and one bridge the permitted use of evidence. Even abundant evidence, abundant public concern, or abundant allegations cannot eliminate the need to work through classification, through the Constitution’s allocation of powers, through the applicable immunity rule, through any rebuttal, through evidentiary limits, through the particular charges, and through the facts established by the court.

My Answer: In natal astrology, Chariklo is often associated with quiet strength, compassion, healing, and the ability to hold space for others. Its placement may suggest where you offer steady support, maintain healthy boundaries, or create a sense of safety during change. The sign describes the style of these qualities, while the house suggests the area of life in which they may be expressed.

My Conclusion: Chariklo symbolizes the power of a calm, caring presence. Its interpretation is most useful when considered alongside the rest of the natal chart.

Future Outlook: As you reflect on Chariklo’s themes, you may find opportunities to strengthen your boundaries, support others without neglecting yourself, and trust the value of patient, sustained care.

Beyond the stars (a whisper sings
[of endless nights {and hidden things
(beyond the reach [of all we know
{where countless distant wonders glow}])}]),
the infinite has no last shore;
however far we go, there’s more.

It means no end to count or find,
no final number, edge, or line.
We understand the words we say,
yet cannot see the whole array.

Can endless space be truly real?
What would forever’s passing feel?
Our minds can trace its signs and still
leave its vastness beyond our skill.

The
Atlantic
Charter,
announced
by
Franklin
D.
Roosevelt
and
Winston
Churchill
in
August
1941,
set
out
eight
principles
for
a
more
peaceful
world
after
the
Second
World
War.

First,
the
United
States
and
Britain
declared
that
they
sought
no
territorial
gains
from
the
war.

Second,
they
opposed
territorial
changes
that
did
not
reflect
the
freely
expressed
wishes
of
the
people
concerned.

Third,
they
affirmed
the
right
of
people
to
choose
their
own
form
of
government.
They
also
called
for
the
restoration
of
sovereign
rights
and
self-government
to
those
who
had
been
deprived
of
them
by
force.

This
principle
became
closely
associated
with
self-determination:
the
idea
that
people
should
have
a
voice
in
their
political
future.
Its
application,
however,
was
contested.
Churchill
did
not
initially
accept
that
it
applied
generally
to
British
colonies,
although
anticolonial
movements
later
used
the
Charter
to
support
their
demands
for
independence.

Fourth,
the
Charter
called
for
all
countries,
large
and
small,
to
enjoy
access
on
equal
terms
to
trade
and
the

Fifth,

economic
cooperation
among
nations
to
improve
labor
standards,
advance

and

greater
social

Sixth,
it
envisioned
a
peace
in
which
all
nations
could
live
safely
within
their
own
boundaries
and
people
everywhere

live

from
fear
and

Seventh,
it
called
for
freedom
of
the
seas,
so
that
people
and
goods

travel
across

without
unnecessary

Eighth,
it
called
for
the
abandonment
of
the
use
of
force
and
the
disarmament
of
nations
that
threatened
aggression.
It
also
looked
toward
a
wider
and
lasting
system
of
general
security.

Together,
these
principles
helped
shape
the
idea
of
collective
security:
countries
working
together
to
prevent
aggression
and
protect
peace.
The
Charter
was
not
itself
a
binding
treaty,
but
its
ideas
influenced
the
later
creation
of
the
United
Nations
